hook.text: Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean but support 25% of all marine species.

buildup.text: Corals share their bodies with algae that give them food and bright colors.

discovery.text: When water gets too warm, corals expel the algae and turn white — called bleaching.

twist.text: Bleached corals can recover if water cools fast. But heat waves last longer now.

climax.text: Half the world's reefs have already died. At 2°C of warming, 99% could vanish.

punchline.text: The rainforests of the sea are bleaching to bone.

quiz.question: What percentage of marine species depend on coral reefs?

details.summary: Mass coral bleaching events are accelerating as ocean temperatures rise, with back-to-back bleaching in 2016, 2017, and 2020 killing over half the coral on parts of the Great Barrier Reef. Without rapid emission reductions, most tropical reefs may be functionally dead by 2050.
details.whyItMatters: Coral reefs are among the first major ecosystems to face climate-driven collapse. Their loss would devastate marine biodiversity and half a billion livelihoods.
takeaways: Mass bleaching events are now occurring roughly every six years
The Great Barrier Reef lost over half its coral between 2016 and 2020
Limiting warming to 1.5 degrees gives some reefs a chance to survive

faq.question: What exactly happens during coral bleaching?
faq.answer: Corals expel symbiotic algae called zooxanthellae when stressed by warm water. Without these algae, corals lose their color and their primary food source. If temperatures remain elevated for weeks, the coral starves and dies.

faq.question: Can coral reefs adapt to warmer temperatures?
faq.answer: Some coral species show limited heat tolerance, and researchers are breeding heat-resistant varieties. However, the pace of warming far exceeds evolutionary adaptation rates, and repeated bleaching events leave no recovery time between events.
